paragraphs.heading: Dry summers, wet winters
paragraphs.text: A Mediterranean climate, also called a dry summer climate, is a temperate type found in the lower mid-latitudes, usually 30 to 45 degrees north or south. Its summers are typically hot and dry and its winters mild and wet. How strongly a place shows these traits depends on its distance from the ocean, its elevation and where it sits. These zones usually lie along the western coasts of landmasses.

paragraphs.heading: Named after one sea
paragraphs.text: The climate takes its name from the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea, most of which share it. It also appears in Atlantic Iberia and northwest Africa, on the Pacific coasts of the United States and Chile, at the southwest tip of South Africa, in parts of southern Australia and in parts of Central Asia. These regions tend to sit next to desert and semi-arid climates, with oceanic climates on their poleward side.

paragraphs.heading: What keeps summers dry
paragraphs.text: The main cause is the subtropical ridge, which shifts toward the pole in summer and back toward the equator in winter. In summer, sinking air over the region brings clear skies and heat, and the ridge keeps conditions very dry with little cloud. In winter the ridge moves away, and travelling storm systems with fronts bring rain. As a result, nearly all rain falls in winter and spring, and four to six months of summer and early fall can pass with no significant rain.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the Köppen code
paragraphs.text: Köppen's code for this climate is Cs. The C marks a temperate climate and the s marks dry summers. A third letter shows summer heat: Csa, the hot dry-summer type, has a warmest month above 22 °C, while Csb, the cool dry-summer type, stays below 22 °C. Both are often just called Mediterranean.

paragraphs.heading: Same pattern, different feel
paragraphs.text: Within this pattern, places differ a lot. Funchal has mild to warm winters with almost no frost or snow, while Tashkent gets frost and snow every winter. Seville has high summer temperatures, but San Francisco's summer highs sit around 21 °C because cold water keeps welling up along the coast. In coastal California the cold current also steadies the air, lowering the chance of rain and often bringing thick sea fog that usually clears by midday.

paragraphs.heading: Plant cover, wine and olives
paragraphs.text: Each region has its own name for its typical plant cover: garrigue or maquis around the Mediterranean, chaparral in California, fynbos in South Africa, mallee in Australia and matorral in Chile. These lands have long grown the Mediterranean trinity of wheat, grapes and olives. That is why they are known for fine wines, olive and grapeseed oils, and bread.
